title: If, then
objectives: Read an implication, its converse and its contrapositive, and tell which ones say the same thing.

screens.title: Four tickets
screens.prose: A compliance rule: **if a trade is over £10,000, it has a second signature**. Each ticket shows a trade's size on one side and its signatures on the other. You see one side of each.
screens.question: Which tickets must you turn over to check the rule? Tap each one.

hints.text: Which hidden sides could show a trade that breaks the rule?
A broken rule needs a trade over £10,000 with only one signature.
Turn the £12,000 ticket to see its signatures, and the 1 signature ticket to see its size.

feedback.correct: The £12,000 ticket and the 1 signature ticket. Only they could hide a breach.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the tickets whose hidden side could break the rule.

byKey.confirm: You turned the 2 signatures ticket. Whatever its size, it has a second signature, so it keeps the rule. The 1 signature ticket could hide a large trade.
byKey.big-only: You turned the £12,000 ticket, which is right. The 1 signature ticket could also hide a trade over £10,000.
byKey.c3k: The £3,000 trade is not over £10,000, so the rule says nothing about it.
byKey.sig2: The 2 signatures ticket has a second signature, so it keeps the rule whatever its size.

explain.text: The rule fails only for a trade over £10,000 with one signature. The £12,000 ticket might have one signature, and the 1 signature ticket might be over £10,000. The other two cannot break the rule, whatever is on the back.

canvas.caption: Only these two could hide a breach

screens.title: If, then
screens.prose: Write $P$ for “the trade is over £10,000” and $Q$ for “it has a second signature”. The rule is $P \Rightarrow Q$, read “if $P$ then $Q$”. $P$ is the **hypothesis** and $Q$ the **conclusion**.
screens.question: For each kind of trade, is the rule kept? Write T or F.

hints.text: Only one kind of trade breaks the rule.
A breach is a trade over £10,000 without a second signature: $P$ true, $Q$ false.
That is the T, F row. Every other row keeps the rule.

feedback.correct: T, F, T, T. The rule fails only when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Mark F only where a trade actually breaks the rule.

byKey.r2c2: A small trade with two signatures breaks nothing. The rule speaks only about trades over £10,000.
byKey.r3c2: A small trade with one signature breaks nothing. The rule makes no demand on small trades.
byKey.r1c2: A trade over £10,000 with one signature is exactly what the rule forbids.
byKey.r0c2: A large trade with a second signature does what the rule asks.

explain.text: $P \Rightarrow Q$ is false only on the T, F row: a large trade with one signature. When $P$ is false the rule asks nothing, so it cannot be broken. Those rows are T.

screens.title: Where the rule breaks
screens.prose: Circle $P$ holds the trades over £10,000; circle $Q$ holds the trades with a second signature.

params.universe: All trades. P: over £10,000. Q: a second signature.

screens.question: Tap the region where a trade breaks the rule $P \Rightarrow Q$.

hints.text: A breach is a trade with $P$ true and $Q$ false.
That trade is inside circle $P$ but outside circle $Q$.
The part of $P$ outside $Q$ is the only breaking region.

feedback.correct: The part of $P$ outside $Q$: large trades with one signature.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the trades inside $P$ but outside $Q$.

byKey.AB: Those trades are large and have a second signature. They keep the rule.
byKey.B: Those trades are small with two signatures. The rule makes no demand on them.
byKey.none: Those trades are small with one signature. The rule says nothing about small trades.

explain.text: The rule fails only in the part of $P$ outside $Q$. When the rule holds, that region is empty, so circle $P$ sits inside circle $Q$.

canvas.caption: The only region that breaks $P \Rightarrow Q$

screens.title: Only if
screens.prose: The desk manual puts the same rule another way: **a trade is over £10,000 only if it has a second signature**.

params.universe: All trades. P: over £10,000. Q: a second signature.

screens.question: Which says the same as “$P$ only if $Q$”?

options.text: $P \Rightarrow Q$
$Q \Rightarrow P$
options.why: You read “only if” as “if”. “$P$ only if $Q$” says $P$ cannot happen without $Q$, so $P$ forces $Q$.

options.text: $P \Leftrightarrow Q$
options.why: That claims both directions. “Only if” gives one direction, from $P$ to $Q$.

options.text: $\lnot P \Rightarrow \lnot Q$
options.why: That says small trades lack a second signature. The manual says nothing about small trades.

hints.text: Can a trade be over £10,000 without a second signature, by the manual?
No: a large trade needs $Q$. So $P$ being true forces $Q$.
“$P$ only if $Q$” is $P \Rightarrow Q$, the same shaded region.

feedback.correct: Right. “$P$ only if $Q$” rules out $P$ without $Q$, which is $P \Rightarrow Q$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which region “only if” rules out.

byKey.conv: You read “only if” as “if”. The manual says no large trade lacks a second signature, so $P$ forces $Q$.

explain.text: “$P$ only if $Q$” rules out $P$ happening without $Q$, the shaded region. That is exactly $P \Rightarrow Q$. When both directions hold we write $P \Leftrightarrow Q$, “$P$ if and only if $Q$”.

screens.title: Three relatives
screens.prose: Take $P \Rightarrow Q$: “if $n$ is a multiple of 4, then $n$ is even”. Swapping the parts gives the **converse**. Negating both parts gives the **inverse**. Doing both gives the **contrapositive**.

params.universe: Whole numbers 1 to 12. P: a multiple of 4. Q: even.

screens.question: Place each sentence beside its name.

tokens.text: If $n$ is even, then $n$ is a multiple of 4
If $n$ is not even, then $n$ is not a multiple of 4
If $n$ is not a multiple of 4, then $n$ is not even
If $n$ is a multiple of 4, then $n$ is not even

hints.text: Name the parts first: $P$ is “a multiple of 4” and $Q$ is “even”.
The converse starts with $Q$. The contrapositive starts with not $Q$.
Converse: if even, then a multiple of 4. Contrapositive: if not even, then not a multiple of 4. Inverse: if not a multiple of 4, then not even.

feedback.correct: Right. One sentence is left over: it negates only the conclusion.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write each sentence as letters first, then match the pattern.

byKey.conv: Check the converse: it swaps the parts and negates nothing.
byKey.contra: Check the contrapositive: it swaps the parts and negates both.
byKey.inv: Check the inverse: it keeps the order and negates both.
byKey.neg: That sentence negates only the conclusion. It matches none of the three patterns.

explain.text: The converse swaps $P$ and $Q$. The inverse negates both and keeps the order. The contrapositive does both.

screens.title: Which ones agree
screens.prose: A truth table settles which relatives say the same thing as $P \Rightarrow Q$. Use the rule you found: an implication is F only when its hypothesis is T and its conclusion is F.

params.universe: Whole numbers 1 to 12. P: a multiple of 4. Q: even.

screens.question: Fill in the converse and the contrapositive.

hints.text: For $Q \Rightarrow P$, the hypothesis is $Q$. Find the row where $Q$ is T and $P$ is F.
For $\lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P$, find the row where $\lnot Q$ is T and $\lnot P$ is F.
The converse is F only on the F, T row. The contrapositive is F only on the T, F row.

feedback.correct: The contrapositive matches $P \Rightarrow Q$ on every row. The converse does not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each column, find the one row where its hypothesis is T and its conclusion F.

byKey.r1c3: On the T, F row the converse's hypothesis $Q$ is F, so the converse is T there.
byKey.r2c3: On the F, T row the converse has $Q$ true and $P$ false, so it is F.
byKey.r1c4: On the T, F row, $\lnot Q$ is T and $\lnot P$ is F, so the contrapositive is F.
byKey.r2c4: On the F, T row, $\lnot Q$ is F, so the contrapositive is T.

explain.text: The contrapositive reads T, F, T, T, the same as $P \Rightarrow Q$. The converse reads T, T, F, T, so it is a different statement. The inverse agrees with the converse, since it is the converse's contrapositive.

screens.title: The converse fails
screens.prose: “If $n$ is a multiple of 4, then $n$ is even” is true. Its converse is “if $n$ is even, then $n$ is a multiple of 4”.

params.universe: Whole numbers 1 to 12. P: a multiple of 4. Q: even.

screens.question: Which value of $n$ shows the converse is false?

options.why: 4 is even and a multiple of 4. It agrees with the converse.
7 is not even, so the converse's hypothesis fails. The converse makes no claim about 7.
12 is even and a multiple of 4. It agrees with the converse.

hints.text: A counterexample makes the hypothesis true and the conclusion false.
You need an even number that is not a multiple of 4.
6 is even, and $6 \div 4 = 1.5$ is not whole.

feedback.correct: 6 is even but not a multiple of 4, so the converse fails.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look in the part of the even circle outside the multiples of 4.

byKey.seven: You picked an odd number. The converse speaks only about even numbers, so 7 cannot break it.

explain.text: A counterexample sits where the converse's hypothesis holds and its conclusion fails. Here that is even numbers that are not multiples of 4: 2, 6 and 10. One is enough.

screens.title: A tempting argument
screens.prose: A researcher says: “If a strategy is overfit, its backtest looks excellent. This backtest looks excellent. So the strategy is overfit.”

state.caption: If the rule holds, the shaded region is empty

screens.question: Is the argument valid?

options.text: No. It runs the rule backwards, from conclusion to hypothesis
Yes. The backtest matches what the rule describes
options.why: You used the rule backwards. It says overfit leads to excellent, not excellent leads to overfit.

options.text: No. Overfit strategies do not always look excellent
options.why: You attacked the first sentence. Grant it as true: the argument still fails.

options.text: Yes. Every excellent backtest comes from an overfit strategy
options.why: That is the converse, which the researcher never stated. A sound strategy can also look excellent.

hints.text: Write the rule as $P \Rightarrow Q$. Which part did the researcher observe?
They observed $Q$, the conclusion, and inferred $P$.
A strategy can sit inside “looks excellent” but outside “overfit”. The rule allows that.

feedback.correct: Right. Knowing $Q$ tells you nothing about $P$ when the rule is $P \Rightarrow Q$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Grant the rule, then ask whether a sound strategy could also look excellent.

byKey.valid: You swapped the hypothesis and the conclusion. The rule gives overfit $\Rightarrow$ excellent, not excellent $\Rightarrow$ overfit. This slip is called affirming the converse.

explain.text: The rule puts “overfit” inside “looks excellent”. A strategy in the rest of “looks excellent” is sound and still has a fine backtest. Concluding $P$ from $Q$ is affirming the converse.

canvas.caption: Excellent backtests that are not overfit

screens.title: A quiet Monday
screens.prose: On Monday the desk did 17 trades. None was over £10,000. The counts are in the circles.
screens.question: Was the rule “if a trade is over £10,000, it has a second signature” kept on Monday?

options.text: Yes. No trade was over £10,000, so none could break it
No. The rule was never tested, so it fails
options.why: You took an untested rule as broken. A breach needs a large trade with one signature, and there was none.

options.text: Neither. The rule is not a statement on such a day
options.why: The rule is still a statement on Monday. It is true, because no trade breaks it.

options.text: No. 14 trades had only one signature
options.why: You counted small trades with one signature. The rule asks nothing of small trades.

hints.text: Which region holds the breaches?
Breaches sit inside “Over £10,000” but outside “Two signatures”.
That region holds 0 trades, so nothing broke the rule.

feedback.correct: Yes. With a false hypothesis, the implication is true.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the trades in the breaking region.

byKey.fourteen: You counted the 14 small trades with one signature. The rule makes no demand on small trades.

explain.text: The breaking region holds no trades, so the rule was kept. An implication whose hypothesis never holds is **vacuously true**. Every row with $P$ false is T.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose:
$P \Rightarrow Q$ is false only when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false. Your table showed:

$$P \Rightarrow Q \text{ agrees with } \lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P \text{ on every row}$$

The converse $Q \Rightarrow P$ is a different statement.
screens.question: Which says the same as “if the price is above £100, the alert fires”?

options.text: If the alert does not fire, the price is not above £100
If the alert fires, the price is above £100
options.why: That is the converse. The alert might fire for another reason.

options.text: If the price is not above £100, the alert does not fire
options.why: That is the inverse. It agrees with the converse, not with the rule.

options.text: The price is above £100 and the alert does not fire
options.why: That sentence describes a breach of the rule. It is the rule's negation, met in the next lesson.

feedback.correct: Right. That is the contrapositive, so it says the same thing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Negate both parts and swap them.

byKey.conv: You swapped the parts but did not negate them. That is the converse, a different statement.

explain.text: Negating both parts and swapping them gives the contrapositive. It fails on exactly the same row as the rule: price above £100, alert silent.

screens.title: A margin rule
screens.prose: A broker's rule: **if an account falls below £25,000, new trades are blocked**. Each card is one account record: its balance on one side, its trading status on the other.
screens.question: Which records must the auditor turn over? Tap each one.

hints.text: A breach is an account below £25,000 that can still trade.
Which visible sides could belong to such an account?
The £18,000 record might say Allowed, and the Allowed record might be below £25,000.

feedback.correct: The £18,000 record and the Allowed record.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn only the records whose hidden side could show a breach.

byKey.confirm: You turned the Blocked record. A blocked account keeps the rule whatever its balance. The Allowed record could hide a low balance.
byKey.c40k: £40,000 is not below £25,000, so the rule makes no demand on that account.
byKey.blocked: A blocked account keeps the rule whatever its balance.

explain.text: A breach is $P$ true and $Q$ false: a low balance with trading allowed. Only the £18,000 record and the Allowed record could hide one.

ideas: $P \Rightarrow Q$ is false only when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false. When $P$ is false it is true, vacuously.
The contrapositive $\lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P$ says the same as $P \Rightarrow Q$. The converse $Q \Rightarrow P$ and the inverse do not.
“$P$ only if $Q$” is $P \Rightarrow Q$. $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ claims both directions.

formula.name: Contrapositive
formula.tex: P \Rightarrow Q \;\text{ agrees with }\; \lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P
formula.note: To test $P \Rightarrow Q$, check the cases with $P$ true and the cases with $Q$ false.

summary.trap: Seeing the conclusion does not prove the hypothesis: from $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $Q$ you cannot conclude $P$.

quiz.prose: The margin rule: if an account falls below £25,000, new trades are blocked.
quiz.question: Which statement says the same thing?

options.text: If new trades are not blocked, the account is not below £25,000
If new trades are blocked, the account is below £25,000
options.why: That is the converse. An account could be blocked for another reason.

options.text: If the account is not below £25,000, new trades are not blocked
options.why: That is the inverse. It agrees with the converse, not with the rule.

options.text: The account is below £25,000 and new trades are not blocked
options.why: That describes a breach. It is what the rule forbids.

feedback.correct: Right. The contrapositive says the same as the rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Negate both parts and swap them.

explain.text: The rule fails only for a low balance with trading allowed. The contrapositive fails in exactly that case, so the two agree.

quiz.prose: Consider “if $n$ is even, then $n$ is a multiple of 4”, for whole numbers $n \ge 1$.
quiz.question: What is the smallest $n$ that shows the statement is false?

widget.label: Smallest counterexample
widget.accept: 2: even, and not a multiple of 4

feedback.correct: 2. It is even and not a multiple of 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test 1, 2, 3, ... until the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails.

byKey.six: 6 is a counterexample, but a smaller one exists.
byKey.one: 1 is odd, so the hypothesis fails. It cannot break the statement.
byKey.four: 4 is even and a multiple of 4. It agrees with the statement.

explain.text: 1 is odd, so it makes the hypothesis false. 2 is even and not a multiple of 4, so it breaks the statement. It is the smallest such number.

quiz.prose: $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ means $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $Q \Rightarrow P$ both hold.
quiz.question: On which rows is $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ true?

options.text: T, T and F, F: where $P$ and $Q$ have the same value
T, T only
options.why: You treated it like **and**. On the F, F row both implications are vacuously true.

options.text: Every row except T, F
options.why: That is $P \Rightarrow Q$ alone. The F, T row breaks $Q \Rightarrow P$.

options.text: T, F and F, T
options.why: Those are the rows where the values differ, and one implication fails on each.

feedback.correct: Right. $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ is true exactly when $P$ and $Q$ match.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the rows where neither implication fails.

explain.text: $P \Rightarrow Q$ fails on T, F and $Q \Rightarrow P$ fails on F, T. Both hold on the other two rows, where $P$ and $Q$ match.

quiz.prose: “You may trade options only if you have passed the options exam.”
quiz.question: Which implication is this?

options.text: If you may trade options, then you have passed the exam
If you have passed the exam, then you may trade options
options.why: You read “only if” as “if”. Passing may be needed but not enough, for example without a licence.

options.text: If you have not passed the exam, you may still trade options
options.why: That contradicts the rule: without the exam you may not trade.

options.text: You may trade options if and only if you have passed the exam
options.why: That adds the other direction, which the rule does not state.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the rule forbids.

explain.text: The rule forbids trading options without the exam. That is $P$ true and $Q$ false, the one row $P \Rightarrow Q$ rules out.
